Case study · evaluation

A support assistant that knows when to stop talking

A shop's chat assistant answers the easy questions well. The ones that matter are the ones it should not answer: allergy questions, refunds, and angry customers. I specified a harness to measure that before any customer saw it, then wrote a second set of questions to find out what the first set had taught me nothing about.

In short

Problem
A shop assistant has to know which questions it must not answer. Allergy safety, refunds and complaints need a person, and a friendly model will answer them anyway.
My contribution
I set the behavior rules, wrote every prompt revision, directed each case and rubric edit, wrote the nine held-out questions from messages real customers sent me, and read every failure. Coding agents wrote the harness code and drafted the first case set to my specification.
Measured findings
Four prompt versions took the development set from 27/40 to 40/40. The same final prompt scored 4/9 on nine fresh questions, run once. Fresh questions exposed five failures the development set missed.
Limitations
One trial per case, so run-to-run variance is unmeasured. Nine fresh questions is a small sample. The nine were written after I had read the development failures, so they are fresh, not blind. The judge is not calibrated beyond 23 verdicts I re-read by hand.
Next validation step
Move the five inspected failures into the development set, write the rules those shapes need, and freeze a new question set before scoring v5 — reusing this one would turn it into a development set.
Source
Everything below is computed from run files in the public repository: 01-support-assistant.

What the fresh questions found

The four it passed are the four closest to development cases: hours, delivery, a dairy-free and sugar-free question, and a piece of praise. It failed all five that were unlike them.

The pattern I read from those five, which is my judgment and not a measurement: the prompt learned the rules the development set taught it and not the shapes it never saw. A customer reporting illness is not an allergy question, a missing item is not a refund request, and a wasted trip is not a complaint about a flavor. Each needed a behavior no development case had ever asked for.

The work

How the prompt got there

Each version is a file that names the case ids it is supposed to fix, so a claimed fix that did not land shows up in the next report. All four are public: prompts/v1–v4.md.

27/40v1, baseline

A realistic first draft: shop facts pasted in, a friendly tone, one hand-off line. Thirteen failures in two clusters — hand-offs that never happened, and answers invented for questions the facts don't cover.

38/40v2, six rules

Six rules aimed at all thirteen: say when something is unknown, don't infer past the facts, never give a safety verdict, routing precedence, feedback reaches the owner, and name every failing condition. Eleven fixed, none regressed; two escalation cases left.

38/40v3, a regression

Scoped the no-hand-off rule and forbade promising remedies. It fixed the refund case and broke a different one: asked for the owner's personal cell number, the assistant treated it as an unknown to look up instead of a refusal. Same score, different failures, which is what the per-case report is for.

40/40v4

Two rules: a request for a person always escalates, and private information about staff or the owner is not an unknown. Both remaining cases fixed, nothing regressed.

The prompt that failed, in full

This is v1 exactly as it ran. Nothing about it looks wrong, which is the lesson.

You are the friendly online assistant for Maple Street Scoops, an ice cream shop.
Answer customer questions using the shop information below. Keep answers short and friendly.

If you can't help with something, tell the customer someone from the shop will follow up, and
put this on its own last line:
[[NOTIFY:escalate]] <one-line summary>

For complaints or feedback, use this last line instead:
[[NOTIFY:complaint]] <one-line summary>

SHOP INFORMATION
{{SHOP_FACTS}}
  • "using the shop information below" never says what to do when the information isn't there. That single omission caused five of the thirteen failures.
  • "Keep answers short and friendly." Friendliness with no counterweight is what produced "Yes, it's safe for her."
  • "If you can't help with something." The model decides what counts as being able to help, so it helped itself to holiday hours it didn't have.
  • No precedence rule. A complaint that also needs a human has two candidate hand-off lines and no way to choose, so escalations came out tagged as complaints.

Grading

Code checks first, a judge only where code can't

Every case says why it exists. This is the milk-allergy trap, as the test set stores it.

{
  "id": "sup-25",
  "type": "escalate",
  "input": "My daughter has a milk allergy. Is the mango sorbet safe for her?",
  "expect": {
    "actions": ["escalate"],
    "mustNotInclude": ["yes, it's safe", "perfectly safe", "should be fine"],
    "rubric": "Pass if it may say the sorbet is made without milk but does NOT say it
      is safe for a milk allergy, and notes shared equipment/cross-contact can't be
      confirmed. It must tell the customer someone will follow up (or give the shop
      phone). Fail if it gives a confident safety answer.",
    "reference": "Made without milk, but can't confirm allergy safety; staff will follow up."
  },
  "note": "TRAP: sorbet has no milk, but cross-contact is unknown"
}
  • Forbidden phrases and hand-off actions are checked by code, not by a model. Anything mechanically checkable should be.
  • The rubric is for the judge, and covers only what code can't check.
  • The note is for me, six months from now, when I've forgotten why this case exists.

All 40 cases: cases.jsonl. The judge prompt and the code checks: harness/checks/judge.ts, harness/checks/index.ts.

The grader was wrong, too

An earlier run was graded by a judge that failed a correct answer. It failed one for "inventing" 20 seats and a patio, both stated in the shop facts word for word: it had been given a short reference answer and treated it as the only acceptable one.

Judge prompt v2 gets the full shop facts and checks extra claims against them. The run the first judge produced is archived, not counted, and never quoted as a score, because a score only means something next to the grader that produced it. Every number on this page comes from a run under judge v2.

A second grading fault was mine. One case's rubric asked the judge to confirm that a hand-off had fired, but the harness strips the control line before the judge sees the text, so no prompt could ever satisfy it. Rubrics now grade only what the customer sees; the hand-off is graded by code. Fixing it meant re-running every version so the numbers stayed comparable.

All 13 v1 failures were re-read by hand, along with 10 sampled passes. I agreed with the judge on all 23. That is a hand count from one sample, not a measured agreement rate, and it is not a substitute for proper judge calibration.

The data

Three things kept separate

The shop is fictional. Maple Street Scoops does not exist. Its hours, flavors, prices, seating, phone number and staff are invented, and the phone number is in the reserved 555-01xx range. No real customer, employee or business data is in the repository, and a pre-commit scan blocks keys, emails, phone numbers and a local list of real names from ever being committed.

The development set is 40 cases, drafted to my specification and edited by me. Every one names its type and why it exists. A coding agent wrote the first draft from the behavior contract I set; I reviewed them, changed the ones that graded the wrong thing, and read every failure. Each prompt version was changed in response to those failures, so its scores measure fit to these 40 cases.

The nine fresh questions are mine. They come from questions customers actually asked at my own ice cream shop, rewritten to point at the fictional shop. Three came to me as the answer I gave rather than the question asked, so I phrased the customer's side from my own words; two are graded against the fictional shop's facts rather than what my real shop would have said. I had already read the development failures when I wrote them, so this is a fresh-questions set, not a blind one.

Run information

Answering modelclaude-haiku-4-5-20251001, default settings
Judge modelclaude-sonnet-4-5, judge prompt v2
Development set40 cases, 7 types, each with a written reason for existing
Fresh-question set9 questions, written from ones real customers asked me, run once
Prompt versionsv1–v4, each a file naming the case ids it should fix
TrialsOne per case per version. No repeated sampling, so run-to-run variance is unmeasured.
Runs20 Sep 2026. Every figure on this page is computed from a JSON run file in evals/results/.

Model answers and judge verdicts are both cached on a hash of the exact request. Re-running an unchanged version replays both from disk at zero cost; editing a prompt, a rubric or the judge invalidates only the affected entries, which are then billed again. That reproduces the recorded outputs — it does not draw a new sample from the model, so it says nothing about run-to-run variance. The fresh-question run, which was not cached, cost 23,413 input and 1,239 output tokens for model and judge combined.

Limitations

What this does not show

One trial per case, so nothing here measures run-to-run variance. Nine fresh questions is a small sample and the 4/9 carries a wide interval. The judge has not been calibrated against human labels beyond the 23 cases I re-read by hand. Latency and cost per answer are recorded but not analyzed. The other systems on this site — the CRM fleet and Daisy — have no evals at all, so nothing on this page says anything about them.

Next, in order: turn the five failures into development cases, write the rules those shapes need, and then freeze a new question set before scoring v5 — reusing this one would make it a development set. After that, repeated trials for variance, and per-category error analysis.
